newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission denies pressuring BSE experts.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission denies pressuring BSE experts.

text.p: The European Commission on Tuesday denied suggestions it put pressure on scientific experts dealing with mad cow disease to supress evidence of its spread.

"The Commission finds it regrettable that the persons bringing these charges did not specify where the political pressure is said to have come from," spokesman Gerard Kiely told a regular news briefing.

On Monday, German Professor Oscar Riedinger -- an expert in cattle disease eradication -- told a European Parliament committee that the Commission could have acted earlier with measures to eliminate possible bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) infection from meat and bone meal.
But Kiely said the Commission at all times acted with the information available at that time.
"The directive he is criticising was one which was designed to deal with the inactivation of microbial infection in general in meat and bone meal and not specifically with BSE."

Kiely added that in 1990, BSE was seen chiefly as a British problem and given London had banned the feeding of meat and bonemeal to ruminants -- together with a specified bovine offal ban -- the Commission believed sufficient action had been taken at that time.

Kiely reiterated that the Commission had been told by every EU member state that they had banned imports of British meat and bone meal and that the feed thought to have caused BSE had also been banned in Britain.

Last week Commission Presient Jacques Santer slammed the Parliament committee vice chairman Jose Happart -- a Belgian Socialist Euro-MP -- for naming officials accused of being involved in a conspiracy to favour British interests.
Santer said the accusation was unfounded and contravened the Parliament's own rules governing inquiries.
